t:
(a) In General.—There shall be available from the Highway Trust Fund (other than the Mass Transit Account) for the Secretary of Transportation to pay the administrative expenses of the National Highway Traffic Administration in carrying out the highway safety programs authorized by sections 157 and 163 of chapter 1 of title 23, United States Code, and sections 402, 403, 405, and 410 of chapter 4 of such title, the National Driver Register under chapter 303 of title 49, United States Code, the motor vehicle safety program under chapter 301 of such title 49, and the motor vehicle information and cost savings program under part C of subtitle VI of such title 49 $4,125,000 for the period of July 30, 2005, through August 14, 2005. 
    (b) Contract Authority.—Funds made available by this section shall be available for obligation in the same manner as if such funds were apportioned under chapter 1 of title 23, United States Code; except that such funds shall remain available until expended.

fable.w: This section only makes Highway Trust Fund money available for a federal agency's administrative expenses and specifies how those funds may be obligated. The tempting reading is that the referenced highway safety programs involve states, but nothing in this section calls for consultation, comment, hearings, advisory bodies, or a right to sue involving any party outside the federal government. It is purely a funding provision.
fable.s: There shall be available from the Highway Trust Fund (other than the Mass Transit Account) for the Secretary of Transportation to pay the administrative expenses of the National Highway Traffic Administration

qwen_block.w: This section is an appropriation provision that authorizes the use of federal funds for administrative expenses. It does not involve any consultation, coordination, or decision-making process with parties outside the federal government. The actors involved are the Highway Trust Fund and the Secretary of Transportation, both of which are inside the federal government.
qwen_block.s: There shall be available from the Highway Trust Fund... for the Secretary of Transportation to pay the administrative expenses of the National Highway Traffic Administration

opus.w: This section only makes Highway Trust Fund money available for NHTSA's administrative expenses and says how those funds can be obligated. It may look procedural because of the "Contract Authority" heading and the references to safety programs. But "contract authority" here is budget language about obligating funds. It does not create any consultation, hearing, comment period, advisory body, rulemaking or right to sue that would involve anyone outside the federal government.
opus.s: There shall be available from the Highway Trust Fund (other than the Mass Transit Account) for the Secretary of Transportation to pay the administrative expenses of the National Highway Traffic Administration

qwen_chat.w: This section is a standard appropriations provision that authorizes the availability of funds for administrative expenses. It does not require or recommend any consultation, coordination, or participation with parties outside the federal government (such as the public, states, or experts) before the Secretary makes decisions regarding the use of these funds. The actors involved are solely federal entities (Secretary of Transportation, National Highway Traffic Administration).
qwen_chat.s: There shall be available from the Highway Trust Fund (other than the Mass Transit Account) for the Secretary of Transportation to pay the administrative expenses of the National Highway Traffic Administration...
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the funds are for "administrative expenses" of a program, there is an implicit requirement for public participation in how those funds are spent. However, the text itself only authorizes the appropriation and availability of funds; it does not mandate any specific participatory process (like hearings, comments, or advisory boards) for the expenditure of these funds. The definition requires explicit consultation or coordination with outsiders *before* a decision, which is absent here.
